blogs.title: When Death Threats Aren’t Enough: The Tenth Circuit’s Rigorous Persecution Threshold in Jimenez v. Bondi
blogs.description: Jimenez reaffirms the Tenth Circuit’s view that threats—even repeated, armed, and terrifying ones involving a child—rarely suffice to establish past persecution without physical harm or other concrete indicia of severe suffering. The post unpacks how the panel aggregated the incidents yet still found them wanting under Karki, Ritonga, and related precedents; why the court discounted psychological aftereffects; and what kinds of evidence (e.g., documented attempts at abduction, medical or expert corroboration, contemporaneous reporting) might tip similar cases over the persecution line. It also situates the decision within cross-circuit tensions over whether credible death threats can, standing alone, constitute persecution.

blogs.title: Mixed Motives, Central Reasons: Criminal Retaliation Versus Political Opinion in the Tenth Circuit’s Nexus Analysis
blogs.description: This post focuses on the nexus holding: the court deemed the primary motive to be retaliation for Jimenez’s interference with a narco-trafficking operation, not Petitioners’ Liberal Party activism. Drawing on Rivera-Barrientos, Dallakoti, and the Tenth Circuit’s recent articulation of mixed-motive principles in O.C.V. v. Bondi, the piece explains how timing, perpetrator statements (“snitch” for the prosecutor’s office), and escalation after a property dispute eclipsed politics as a central reason. It offers practitioner takeaways for proving political opinion as a central reason—linking specific persecutor identities to earlier political threats, adducing statements evidencing political animus, and using expert or social media evidence to show targeted opposition activity rather than a purely personal feud.

blogs.title: Unable or Unwilling, or Just Unasked? Failure to Report, Police Apathy, and Internal Relocation in Jimenez
blogs.description: Jimenez applies Singh v. Bondi’s framework by emphasizing notice to the state: minimal reporting and two unhelpful officers did not establish a government “unable or unwilling” to protect, especially where authorities had attempted searches of the property. Citing analogous reasoning from other circuits on isolated police apathy, the court treated the record as counter-evidence to claims of state complicity. The post explores what suffices to prove futility or danger in reporting (systemic corruption evidence, prior reprisals, expert testimony) and shows how that analysis dovetailed with internal-relocation findings—family living safely in Colombia, a three-week safe stay in the countryside, and threats limited to leaving the neighborhood—ultimately undercutting a well-founded fear.

blogs.title: Deference All the Way Down: Substantial Evidence Review and Record-Building Lessons from Jimenez v. Bondi
blogs.description: The decision illustrates how substantial-evidence review, coupled with a single-member BIA affirmance, can be outcome-determinative even when credibility is conceded. This post dissects the appellate posture—why petitioners could not compel a contrary finding on persecution, nexus, or government protection—and highlights strategic litigation gaps: abandoning CAT and due process claims, not developing a particular social group theory, sparse corroboration of political motive, scant documentation of futility in reporting, and limited country-conditions proof of state connivance. It closes with practical guidance for assembling a robust administrative record designed to survive the Tenth Circuit’s deferential lens.
